newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy '98 budget could rise to 28 trln lire - papers.
newsitem.headline: Italy '98 budget could rise to 28 trln lire - papers.

text.p: Italy's 1998 deficit-cutting budget could be as high as 28 trillion lire, some three trillion lire above plan, Italian newspapers reported at the weekend.

Rome-based La Reppublica reported on Saturday that the Italian Treasury was seeking a further three trillion lire of cuts in next year's financial budget to counter an extra three trillion lire of spending.

By Sunday, the Treasury was reported to have said it was premature to talk of holes in the 1998 budget and for now the budget would not be changed. Preparations on the budget will restart at end-August for verification expected in September.

But Milan-based financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore on Sunday said the 1998 budget risked being as high as 27.8 trillion lire due to extra spending on education, the increased number of people taking early retirement pensions and other items.
Turin-based La Stampa said that increased spending would be needed for pensions and education, and that trade unions had said there should be no more cuts in welfare spending.

In late May, Prime Minister Romano Prodi unveiled Italy's three-year economic strategy, known as the DPEF, which outlined that the 1998 budget should slice 25 trillion lire off the state deficit by combining 15 trillion lire of spending cuts with 10 trillion lire of revenue-raising measures.

La Repubblica reported that the budget still planned 10 trillion lire of revenue-raising measures and eight trillion lire of cuts in social welfare spending, but cuts in other areas were likely to rise to 10 trillion lire from a previous understood seven trillion lire.

There was some confusion over the size of the 1998 budget just days before the DPEF was announced back in May with Treasury Minister undersecretary Laura Pennacchi saying Italy needed to make deficit cuts of between 25 and 28 trillion lire in the budget with the number likely to be at the high end of the scale.
